listeningScripts.title: Booking a First Aid Course
listeningScripts.text:
Trainer: Good afternoon, Meadowbank First Aid Training.
Caller: Hello — I'd like to book onto one of your courses. My workplace has asked me to become a first aider.
Trainer: Of course. Can I take your name?
Caller: Yes, it's Bernadette Ellery. Ellery is E-double L-E-R-Y.
Trainer: And a daytime number?
Caller: 07802 447 159.
Trainer: Which course does your employer need?
Caller: I'm not sure. There were two mentioned.
Trainer: The one most employers ask for is the three-day course, which covers workplace first aid in full. There's also a one-day emergency course, which is a shorter version and is not usually accepted where there are more than fifty staff.
Caller: We have about ninety, so it's the three-day one.
Trainer: That's right. The fee is two hundred and ninety pounds, and that includes the manual and the certificate.
Caller: When does the next one run?
Trainer: The next available is the twelfth of June, running Wednesday to Friday. After that it's the ninth of July.
Caller: June is better.
Trainer: I'll hold a place. The course runs nine to five each day, and I should stress that attendance on all three days is required — there's no way to catch up a missed day, because the assessment is continuous.
Caller: Understood. Is there an exam?
Trainer: No written exam. You're assessed throughout on practical demonstrations, and the certificate is valid for three years.
Caller: Do I need to prepare anything?
Trainer: Nothing to study in advance. Wear comfortable clothing, because a good deal of the course is spent kneeling on the floor practising resuscitation.
Caller: Is lunch provided?
Trainer: Tea and coffee, but not lunch — there's a supermarket two minutes away. And do let me know in advance about any injury or condition that would make kneeling difficult, because we can adapt the practical work.
Caller: That's useful, thank you. How do I pay?
Trainer: I'll email an invoice; payment is due seven days before the course starts.

listeningScripts.title: Nature Reserve Visitor Briefing
listeningScripts.text:
Warden: Morning everyone, and welcome to Cranmere Marsh nature reserve. I'm Tom, one of the wardens, and this briefing takes about five minutes before you go out.

First, why the paths matter. This is a wetland, and the ground either side of the boardwalk looks solid and is not — people go in up to the waist most summers, usually while photographing something. Stay on the marked routes. There is also ground-nesting between March and August, and a bird disturbed off a nest in cold weather can lose the whole clutch in twenty minutes.

Dogs are permitted on the outer circuit only, on a lead, and not on the reserve proper. I know that's unpopular. It exists because ground-nesting birds respond to a dog exactly as they would to a fox, whether or not the dog is interested in them.

Now the hides, which is what most of you have come for. The main hide overlooks the largest lagoon and is reached by the boardwalk running straight ahead from this centre. The tower hide is at the northern end of the reserve, and it's the only one with a view over the reedbed — worth the climb in the late afternoon. The small hide beside the pond is on your right as you leave the visitor centre, no more than fifty metres away, and it's the one to use if you have limited time. Toilets are behind the visitor centre. The car park you came through is on the west side, next to the entrance track, and the picnic area is between the car park and the pond.

Two practical points. The reserve floods after heavy rain, and when it does the tower hide becomes unreachable — check the board at the entrance rather than walking up there to find out. And please record what you see in the sightings book by the door. It is not a formality: our count of which species use this reserve, and therefore the case for keeping it, is built from what visitors write down.

listeningScripts.title: Dividing a Recycling Project
listeningScripts.text:
Tutor: So, the recycling behaviour project. Have you divided the work?
Marek: Partly. Sana's doing the household interviews and I'm doing the observation at the recycling points.
Sana: But we've realised the interviews are going to take much longer than we allowed.
Tutor: How many are you planning?
Sana: Forty. Each one is about half an hour, plus travel.
Tutor: That's twenty hours of interviewing before you transcribe anything. What's the deadline?
Marek: Five weeks.
Tutor: Then forty is too many and you should decide that now rather than in week four. What would twenty-five buy you?
Sana: We'd lose some of the comparison between the two neighbourhoods.
Tutor: Would you? You have two neighbourhoods and forty interviews, so twenty each. At twenty-five you'd have twelve or thirteen each, which is thin but workable for a qualitative study, and you'd actually finish.
Marek: I'd rather cut the observation than the interviews.
Tutor: Say more.
Marek: The observation is telling us less than we hoped. People use the recycling point in about fifteen seconds and I can't see what's in the bags.
Tutor: That's an honest finding and you should report it rather than quietly dropping it. A method that didn't work, explained, is worth more than a method that worked and wasn't needed.
Sana: So we keep the observation but write it up as a limitation?
Tutor: Write it up as a finding about method. Then reallocate Marek's time to the interviews, which is what you actually need. And Marek — do the transcription as you go, not at the end.
Marek: Why does that matter?
Tutor: Because if you leave it, you will spend the final week transcribing instead of thinking, and the analysis is the part being marked.

listeningScripts.title: Why Languages Are Lost
listeningScripts.text:
Lecturer: Roughly half the languages spoken today are expected to have no fluent speakers by the end of this century, and I want to spend this session on why that happens, because the mechanism is more specific than "globalisation".

Languages very rarely die because speakers are forbidden to use them, though that has happened. The far commoner path is a shift in domain. A language stops being used in one setting — the workplace, then the school, then the market — while remaining in use at home, and at each stage it becomes less useful to the next generation. The final step is a generation of parents who speak the language to each other and the majority language to their children, and it is usually taken for reasons that are entirely sensible from where those parents stand.

That point matters. Parents shifting language are typically making a rational decision about their children's prospects in an environment where the smaller language carries a penalty — in employment, in schooling, sometimes in how the family is treated. Describing the outcome as carelessness misdescribes both the cause and the remedy.

What is lost is easy to state badly. It is not that a language contains knowledge unavailable in any other, though specific ecological and medical vocabularies do sometimes vanish with it. The stronger claim is about the people: language shift is very often accompanied by measurable harm to community cohesion and to the wellbeing of the generation that loses the ability to speak with its grandparents.

Revitalisation works, and works under conditions that are well understood and hard to supply. Programmes that produce new speakers share three features: the language is used for something other than language teaching, so it becomes the medium rather than the subject; there are settings where it is the only option, because a language that is always optional will lose to the one that is always available; and the community rather than the institution decides how it is used. Programmes lacking those, however well funded, produce students who can pass a test and do not speak.

The honest caveat is about scale. Documentation preserves a record and does not preserve a language. A handful of revitalisation efforts have genuinely reversed shift; most have slowed it; and the difference between those outcomes has more to do with how many children hear the language daily than with any technique available to a linguist.
